We are six weeks from the midterm elections, and voters are starting to lock in to key races. Having just spent time in Texas and North Carolina, I can vouch for the fact that ad spending is pouring in and blanketing America.

   Polling has been spotty this year, but it’s worth checking in on where things stand today . And, as of today, Democrats appear to have a solid edge.

   According to polling averages at RealClear Polling , Democrats have advantages in eight of the nine closest states (the sole GOP edge is in Iowa). According to these averages, Democrats are leading in Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Maine, New Hampshire, Alaska, Georgia and North Carolina.

   So, under that scenario, Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico would pull off the improbable and win Michigan and Texas.

   This type of blue wave all seems a little hard to imagine at this point, and polling has underestimated GOP voters many times before. But it provides a notable benchmark with six weeks left.

   We are committed to offering you the most comprehensive coverage of these midterm elections, and this includes capturing the pulse of the nation in a way that goes beyond polling. That’s why we are thrilled to launch our “Rooted In” series today. In this video series, a number of our journalists will take you back to their hometowns across the United States and offer you the most authentic window into what Americans care about. You will meet business owners and local politicians. You will hear from key voices in these communities and, yes, even a few of our beloved moms. Our series starts today with Josh Jamerson taking us all to Detroit . There are more captivating journeys to come, and we can’t wait to take you home with us.

   This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       People and Policies I’m Watching   Trump’s Monday: President Trump has two policy meetings scheduled this morning, then he is expected to attend a ribbon-cutting ceremony at 1:45 p.m. ET. After that, the president will go to New York, where he will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at 4:10 p.m. Trump will later meet with French President Emmanuel Macron, take part in a Republican National Committee reception and participate in a MAGA Inc. dinner.

   U.N. General Assembly: The United Nations General Assembly meets this week in New York. Trump is scheduled to speak on Tuesday.

       What I’m Following     JON ELSWICK/AP   Trump sets his sights on the International Criminal Court. The Trump administration is preparing to impose sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, according to officials, an escalation in Washington’s efforts to dismantle the institution after it issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The sanctions would forbid most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, which could potentially cripple the court by prohibiting it from conducting transactions in U.S. dollars, cutting it off from much of the global financial system.

   The president says his arch will also have a military purpose. Trump said that his proposed triumphal arch in Washington will also serve as a “military complex” housing drones and sniper ammunition, providing new justification for the planned arch amid ongoing litigation. A federal lawsuit filed by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian has challenged the proposal.

   Frustration is bubbling over for Trump. Twenty months into his second term, the president isn’t getting his way—and he isn’t happy about it , according to advisers, administration officials and others close to him. Behind the scenes, the president has told aides he doesn’t have enough political allies defending him on television and making the case for his second-term achievements, according to people familiar with the matter.

       What Else Is Happening   • CNN, MS NOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration after their journalists were denied entry to the White House. Separately, CNN was removed from a planned assignment representing a rotating pool of TV journalists.

   • Republicans are spending big in a series of battleground states, unleashing one of their biggest advantages over Democrats.

   • With Election Day approaching, Republican worries about voter enthusiasm are spilling beyond swing states into red bastions such as Kansas.

   • Trump’s Greenland deal eases the way for U.S. business on the resource-rich Arctic Island.

   • Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat, is leading the fight against Trump’s Kennedy Center plans.

   • Abdul El-Sayed Battles Politics and Islamophobia ( Detroit Free Press )

Damian Paletta
 
The Midterm Sprint Is Here. Senate Polls Show a Lot of Blue.
 
Plus, Trump says proposed arch will also be a ‘military complex’; and the administration prepares sanctions on International Criminal Court
 
 
SARAH RICE/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Good morning. We are six weeks from the midterm elections, and voters are starting to lock in to key races. Having just spent time in Texas and North Carolina, I can vouch for the fact that ad spending is pouring in and blanketing America.

 

Polling has been spotty this year, but it’s worth checking in on where things stand today. And, as of today, Democrats appear to have a solid edge.

 

According to polling averages at RealClear Polling, Democrats have advantages in eight of the nine closest states (the sole GOP edge is in Iowa). According to these averages, Democrats are leading in Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Maine, New Hampshire, Alaska, Georgia and North Carolina.

 

So, under that scenario, Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico would pull off the improbable and win Michigan and Texas.

 

This type of blue wave all seems a little hard to imagine at this point, and polling has underestimated GOP voters many times before. But it provides a notable benchmark with six weeks left.

 

We are committed to offering you the most comprehensive coverage of these midterm elections, and this includes capturing the pulse of the nation in a way that goes beyond polling. That’s why we are thrilled to launch our “Rooted In” series today. In this video series, a number of our journalists will take you back to their hometowns across the United States and offer you the most authentic window into what Americans care about. You will meet business owners and local politicians. You will hear from key voices in these communities and, yes, even a few of our beloved moms. Our series starts today with Josh Jamerson taking us all to Detroit. There are more captivating journeys to come, and we can’t wait to take you home with us.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Trump’s Monday: President Trump has two policy meetings scheduled this morning, then he is expected to attend a ribbon-cutting ceremony at 1:45 p.m. ET. After that, the president will go to New York, where he will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at 4:10 p.m. Trump will later meet with French President Emmanuel Macron, take part in a Republican National Committee reception and participate in a MAGA Inc. dinner.

 

U.N. General Assembly: The United Nations General Assembly meets this week in New York. Trump is scheduled to speak on Tuesday.

 
 
 

What I’m Following

 
 
JON ELSWICK/AP
 

Trump sets his sights on the International Criminal Court. The Trump administration is preparing to impose sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, according to officials, an escalation in Washington’s efforts to dismantle the institution after it issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The sanctions would forbid most transactions with the ICC after a grace period of six to seven months, which could potentially cripple the court by prohibiting it from conducting transactions in U.S. dollars, cutting it off from much of the global financial system.

 

The president says his arch will also have a military purpose. Trump said that his proposed triumphal arch in Washington will also serve as a “military complex” housing drones and sniper ammunition, providing new justification for the planned arch amid ongoing litigation. A federal lawsuit filed by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian has challenged the proposal.

 

Frustration is bubbling over for Trump. Twenty months into his second term, the president isn’t getting his way—and he isn’t happy about it, according to advisers, administration officials and others close to him. Behind the scenes, the president has told aides he doesn’t have enough political allies defending him on television and making the case for his second-term achievements, according to people familiar with the matter.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• CNN, MS NOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration after their journalists were denied entry to the White House. Separately, CNN was removed from a planned assignment representing a rotating pool of TV journalists.

 

• Republicans are spending big in a series of battleground states, unleashing one of their biggest advantages over Democrats.

 

• With Election Day approaching, Republican worries about voter enthusiasm are spilling beyond swing states into red bastions such as Kansas.

 

• Trump’s Greenland deal eases the way for U.S. business on the resource-rich Arctic Island.

 

• Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat, is leading the fight against Trump’s Kennedy Center plans.
